analysis.investment_thesis: KSH International scores poorly on Greenblatt's Magic Formula: earnings yield of ~3.5% (EBIT INR 118 Cr / EV ~INR 3,381 Cr) is well below the 6% minimum threshold, meaning the market is pricing in perfection. Despite decent ROCE of 39%, persistently negative FCF (-INR 130 Cr in FY25) reveals that reported profits are not translating into real cash generation.
key_strengths: Revenue CAGR of 31% (FY22–25) and EBITDA CAGR of 33% — genuine business momentum in a power/renewables cycle
Reported ROCE of 39.39% suggests efficient use of operating capital, a positive Magic Formula signal
High promoter holding (74.58%) and strong FII/DII interest (18.9% combined) reflects institutional conviction
key_risks: Earnings yield of ~3.5% (EBIT/EV) is far below Greenblatt's 12% threshold — the stock is expensive on Magic Formula
Free cash flow deeply negative in 3 of 4 years (FY25: -INR 130 Cr) despite INR 68 Cr net profit — working capital and capex are consuming all earnings
Finance costs growing at 46.3% CAGR vs. revenue at 31% — debt is becoming more expensive faster than the business grows
red_flags: OCF positive only 1/4 years — profits are accounting entries, not cash
Capex surged to INR 120 Cr in FY25 (nearly 2x net profit of INR 68 Cr) — heavy capital intensity destroys FCF conversion
Gross margin of only 10.68% and operating margin of 5.18% — commodity-like pricing power with no real moat
Debt doubled from INR 157 Cr (FY22) to INR 366 Cr (FY25) — growth is largely debt-funded
analysis.detailed_analysis:
Running the Magic Formula: EBIT of INR 118 Cr against an Enterprise Value of ~INR 3,381 Cr (Market Cap INR 3,025 Cr + Debt INR 366 Cr – Cash INR 10 Cr) yields an earnings yield of just 3.5%. Greenblatt requires at least 12% for a stock to rank well — KSHINTL fails this test badly. The P/E of 32x and EV/EBITDA of 18.3x confirm the stock is priced for a high-quality compounder, which the fundamentals don't yet support. ROIC computed on invested capital (~INR 655 Cr) comes to ~18%, decent but not exceptional, and the reported ROCE of 39% may be flattering due to current liabilities netting against the denominator.

The FCF picture is disqualifying for a Greenblatt-style investor: three consecutive negative OCF years, with FY25 FCF of -INR 130 Cr despite INR 68 Cr net profit. This means the business is consuming cash, not generating it — working capital is ballooning alongside revenue (a classic sign of a stretched distribution chain), and capex of INR 120 Cr in FY25 alone equals nearly 2x net income. Finance costs growing at 46% CAGR signal rising debt servicing pressure. Until FCF turns consistently positive and the earnings yield approaches double digits, the Magic Formula gives this a clear pass.
